source.name: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources), monthly
source.attribution: Data obtained from the NASA Langley Research Center POWER Project funded through the NASA Earth Science Directorate Applied Science Program
source.resolution: About 0.5° × 0.625° (about 55 km) for weather variables and 1° for sunshine and clouds: one value describes a whole region, not a single street.
source.period: January 1981 to the last complete year

variables.name: Air temperature
variables.definition: How warm the air is about 2 metres above the ground, averaged over day and night.
variables.why: Rising greenhouse gases warm the air almost everywhere, but not at the same speed: polar regions and dry land warm fastest.
variables.model: MERRA-2 (NASA Global Modeling and Assimilation Office reanalysis)

variables.name: Daytime high temperature
variables.definition: The hottest air temperature of each day (averaged over the month): what afternoons feel like.
variables.why: Hot afternoons matter for health, crops and energy use; cities and deserts often show the clearest increase.

variables.name: Night-time low temperature
variables.definition: The coolest air temperature of each day (averaged over the month), usually just before sunrise.
variables.why: Nights often warm faster than days, especially in cities (the urban heat island) and where the air gets more humid.

variables.name: Rainfall
variables.definition: How much rain (and melted snow) falls, as millimetres per day averaged over the month.
variables.why: Rain shifts with ocean temperatures and climate change: some regions get wetter while others dry out, even from the same cause.
variables.model: MERRA-2, bias-corrected with satellite and gauge rainfall (GPCP / GPM)

variables.name: Relative humidity
variables.definition: How close the air is to being saturated with water vapour (100 % = fog or dew).
variables.why: Warmer air can hold more water, so relative humidity often falls over land as it warms; irrigation can raise it locally.

variables.name: Root-zone soil wetness
variables.definition: How wet the soil is where plant roots live (roughly the top metre): 0 % = completely dry, 100 % = soaked.
variables.why: Drought, heat and changing rain dry soils out; irrigation and wetter climates make them wetter. It is a key signal for farming.

variables.name: Surface soil wetness
variables.definition: How wet the top few centimetres of soil are (0 % = dry, 100 % = soaked): they react quickly to rain and hot days.
variables.why: Responds faster than deep soil, so it tracks short droughts and wet spells.

variables.name: Evapotranspiration (water leaving the land)
variables.definition: The energy used to evaporate water from soil and plants, a measure of how much water the land gives back to the air.
variables.why: More green plants or irrigation raise it; drying soils lower it. It links the water cycle to the energy cycle.

variables.name: Sunshine reaching the ground
variables.definition: How much sunlight energy reaches the surface each day, after clouds and haze have blocked some of it.
variables.why: Air pollution and dust dim the sky; cleaner air or fewer clouds brighten it ("global dimming and brightening").
variables.model: CERES and NASA GEWEX SRB satellite estimates (from 1984)
variables.joined_sources: GEWEX SRB and CERES SYN1deg / FLASHFlux (NASA POWER documentation)

variables.name: Cloud cover
variables.definition: The share of the sky covered by clouds, seen from satellites.
variables.why: Clouds respond to ocean temperatures and circulation changes, and in turn change how much sun warms the ground.
variables.joined_sources: GEWEX SRB and CERES SYN1deg / FLASHFlux (NASA POWER documentation)

variables.name: Wind speed
variables.definition: How fast the wind blows about 2 metres above the ground.
variables.why: Changing weather patterns and new buildings or forests change near-ground wind ("global stilling").

variables.name: Surface air pressure
variables.definition: The weight of the air above a place; high pressure usually brings settled weather, low pressure storms.
variables.why: Shifts in pressure belts move storm tracks and rain belts; trends are small but can be significant.
